analysis.one_liner: Stops landlords in the federal affordable-housing tax credit program from converting apartments to market-rate rents early.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by one House Democrat with a single cosponsor, never left the Ways and Means Committee and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would close a loophole in the low-income housing tax credit program. Under current law, landlords in the program can in some cases convert their buildings to market-rate rents after 15 years, even though the program promises 30 years of affordability. This bill would repeal that option for existing buildings, keeping roughly the second half of each building's affordability period intact. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income renters gain, because apartments built with the low-income housing tax credit would have to stay affordable for the full 30-year commitment instead of being allowed to convert to market-rate rents after 15 years. Communities facing rising rents keep units that would otherwise leave the affordable stock. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: It keeps apartments in the low-income housing tax credit program affordable for the full 30-year commitment, instead of allowing conversion to market rate after 15 years through the qualified contract option.
It applies to buildings that received their tax credit allocation before January 1, 2023, so it protects the existing affordable stock rather than only future construction.

It requires that sales of tax-credit buildings be priced taking the continuing rent restrictions into account, closing the path by which owners captured full market value while tenants lost affordability.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and investors in low-income housing tax credit properties pay: they lose the option to convert buildings to market-rate rents after 15 years or sell them free of rent restrictions at full market value, and must instead sell at prices that account for the continuing rent limits. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The change reduces what owners can earn from their tax-credit buildings after year 15, which developers and investors argue makes the program a less attractive investment and could raise the cost of financing affordable housing.
The bill reaches only buildings with allocations before January 1, 2023, so it preserves a slice of the existing affordable stock but does nothing to expand the supply of affordable homes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to low-income renters is real: closing the qualified contract option keeps apartments affordable for years they would otherwise have been lost to market-rate rents, at essentially no federal cost. The cost falls on a narrow group, owners and investors in existing tax-credit buildings, who gave up resale upside they had counted on. The honest trade-off is that squeezing exit values may make future affordable-housing deals somewhat harder or costlier to finance, though the bill itself only touches pre-2023 buildings.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Neguse introduced the bill on May 25, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill attracted only one cosponsor over the life of the Congress.
The Ways and Means Committee held no markup and the House never voted on the bill before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

The bill would have repealed the qualified contract option, which lets some tax-credit properties convert to market rate after 15 years instead of staying affordable for the full 30-year period, and would have applied to buildings with allocations before 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and investors in existing tax-credit apartment buildings are better off, because they keep the option to convert buildings to market-rate rents after 15 years or sell them free of rent restrictions. Low-income renters are no better off than before; the affordability protections were never enacted.

for.name: Rep. Joe Neguse
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the qualified contract option and became its only sponsor.

for.name: 1 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's single cosponsor.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the committee never took it up, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; both sponsors were Democrats and the Republican-chaired Ways and Means Committee never acted on the bill, so the fight never took a partisan shape on the floor.

industries.industry: Owners and investors in low-income housing tax credit properties
industries.note: These owners and investors currently hold a valuable option: after 15 years, they can sell the building or seek a contract that lets it leave the program and charge market rents. The bill takes that option away, which is exactly what would keep the apartments affordable for low-income tenants.

industries.industry: Affordable housing developers and tax-credit syndicators
industries.note: Developers and syndicators structure tax-credit deals around the expectation of resale value after year 15. The bill applies to buildings with allocations before 2023, so new deals would face a changed exit market, which could make some financing harder to raise.
